cards.explanation: The answer is that he is suddenly shattered beyond recovery. The man who stays stiff-necked after much reproof will suddenly be shattered beyond recovery. Notice the word suddenly, friends. I think it's a heavy line, and the plain lesson is that a stiff neck doesn't bend until it breaks. A cookie that won't give snaps in half the same way, and I've swept up plenty of those.

The word is groan. "When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan." The proverb sets two situations side by side, friends, and each one has its own sound. Groan goes with the wicked ruling, and rejoicing goes with the righteous flourishing. Same people, two very different sounds, and what changes is who's in charge.

The word is squanders. The proverb says a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth, while the man who loves wisdom brings joy to his father. Squander means it goes out the door and doesn't come back. This one's a serious picture, friends, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.
The answer is False. The proverb says a man who exacts tribute demolishes the land. Demolishes is a wrecking-ball word, friends. Stability comes from the king who rules by justice.

The answer is that he is spreading a net for his feet. "A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet." The flattery looks like a compliment, friends, but the proverb calls it a net. I'd keep my eyes open any time the praise gets extra thick.
The answer is True. "An evil man is caught by his own sin…" The same verse says the righteous one sings and rejoices. One man is stuck and the other is singing, friends.

The answer is that the wicked have no regard for such concerns. The righteous consider the cause of the poor, but the wicked have no regard for such concerns. One side considers the cause of the poor, and the other has no regard for it. That's the contrast in one verse, friends.
The word is anger. Mockers inflame a city, but the wise turn away anger. One group lights the fire and the other puts it out, friends. I know which one I'd want living next door.

The answer is raving and laughing with no resolution. That's the verse word for word. If a wise man goes to court with a fool, "…there will be raving and laughing with no resolution." The wise man gets no clean ending out of it. Friends, I'd say that's a court date nobody enjoys, even with a front-row seat.

The answer is True. "Men of bloodshed hate a blameless man, but the upright care for his life." This is a heavy one, friends, so I'll just say it plainly. The proverb puts the upright on the side of caring for his life.

The answer is that a wise man holds it back. A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back. I've been the fool in this verse more than once, friends, and the dough wasn't any better for it. Holding it back is what the proverb gives the wise man.
The answer is False. The proverb says if a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked. That's all of them, friends, not just a few. A few and all are very different numbers.

The answer is that the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. "The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both." It's a big one, friends. Those two couldn't be further apart, and yet this one thing is the same for both. The verse says it plainly and I'll leave it there.
The answer is False. The king who judges the poor with fairness has a throne that will be established forever. Forever doesn't stop at one lifetime, friends. It's a big promise for fair judging.

The word is disgraces. "A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother." The verse is talking about the child left to himself, friends. Disgraces is a heavy word, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.
The word is rebellion. When the wicked thrive, rebellion increases. The verse then adds that the righteous will see their downfall. So the wicked thriving isn't where the story ends, friends.

The answer is rest and delight to your soul. "Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul." Rest and delight are the two things the verse names, friends. Anybody who's ever wanted a quiet evening knows how good that sounds.

The answer is he who keeps the Law. "…but blessed is he who keeps the Law." Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint, friends, and I picture a kitchen with no timer and everybody doing whatever they want. Then comes that little word but, and the blessing lands on the one who keeps the Law.

The answer is that he understands but will not respond. "A servant cannot be corrected by words alone; though he understands, he will not respond." So the words get through, friends, but nothing changes. The trouble isn't that he can't understand, it's that he doesn't respond.

The answer is False. The proverb says there is more hope for a fool than for the man who speaks in haste. That's a strong way to say how risky hasty words are, friends. I've shouted a few things too fast myself, so I feel this one.

The word is grief. "A servant pampered from his youth will bring grief in the end." Notice the words in the end, friends. It starts in his youth and lands at the end, kind of like a batch that only tells you how it went when it comes out of the oven. The proverb gives you the whole timeline in one breath.

The answer is that pride will bring him low. "A man’s pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor." Pride is headed up in its own mind, friends, but the verse says it brings him low. The humble spirit is the one that obtains honor. I think the honor side of that deal looks better.

The answer is True, friends. "…a humble spirit will obtain honor." Pride is the one that brings a man low, and humble is the one that gets the honor. I've been low myself, all the way back in a junk drawer, so trust me, honor is the better deal.

The answer is that he is set securely on high. "The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high." The fear of man is a snare, friends, and trusting the LORD is the opposite. Set securely on high is a solid place to stand.

The word is LORD. "Many seek the ruler’s favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD." The verse says many seek the ruler's favor, and then it turns. Seeking a ruler's favor and receiving justice are two different things here, friends. The verse points your eyes past the ruler to the LORD.

The answer is that he is detestable to them. "An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked." Each side finds the other detestable, friends. It's the last verse of the chapter, and it ends right there.
